corporate_status.note: WBD common stock (Nasdaq: WBD) and its 4.302%/4.693% senior notes (WBDI30/WBDI33) ceased trading and were delisted upon closing. This analysis is a historical/backward-looking record of the standalone WBD business as last reported (10-K FY2025, 10-Q through Q2 2026) and the strategic logic of the acquisition. There is no forward investment case for WBD; readers interested in the combined business going forward should look at SKYD (Skydance Corporation).

overview: Warner Bros. Discovery was a global media and entertainment company formed by the 2022 merger of WarnerMedia (AT&T) and Discovery, Inc., combining Warner Bros.' film/TV studio and HBO with Discovery's global factual/lifestyle cable networks. It operated as effectively two businesses in one: a structurally declining but cash-generative Global Linear Networks segment (TNT, TBS, CNN, Discovery Channel, HGTV, Food Network, international networks/sports) and a growth-oriented Streaming & Studios division (HBO Max, discovery+, Warner Bros. film/TV production, DC Studios, Warner Bros. Games). WBD ceased to exist as an independent public company on 2026-10-06, when Paramount Skydance Corporation completed its acquisition for $31.01666668/share in cash; the combined company now operates as Skydance Corporation (NYSE: SKYD).

business_model.summary: Four revenue types across three segments: distribution fees from pay-TV/DTH/telecom carriage plus direct-to-consumer streaming subscriptions (52% of FY2025 revenue), advertising on linear networks and ad-supported streaming tiers (20%), content licensing/theatrical box office/games/consumer products (26%), and other (studio tours, production services) (2%). FY2025 total revenue was $37.3B, down 5% YoY, reflecting linear decline partly offset by streaming growth.

revenue_streams.name: Content (theatrical, TV licensing, games, IP licensing)
revenue_streams.trend: volatile, tied to film slate timing

segment_mix_fy2025_revenue.note: 131.6M Streaming subscribers at 12/31/2025, +13% YoY; Global ARPU fell 11% as mix shifted to cheaper international/wholesale tiers
theatrical hits incl. A Minecraft Movie, Superman, Sinners, Weapons; first studio in Hollywood history to open 7 consecutive $40M+ domestic openings
still the largest profit pool (73% of segment Adjusted EBITDA) despite -21% EBITDA decline; domestic linear subscribers -9%, audience -25%

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2B and B2C: B2B distribution/carriage deals with cable/DTH/telecom operators and licensing deals with other studios/streamers (including, historically, Netflix); B2C direct subscriptions to HBO Max and discovery+; B2B advertising sales to brands/agencies.
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S.-centric but globalizing - HBO Max expanded past 100 international markets in 2025 and launched in Germany/Italy (Jan 2026) with UK planned for March 2026; majority of Global Linear Networks and legacy affiliate revenue is still domestic.

competitive_position.market_position: Mid-scale global streamer (131.6M subscribers at YE2025) well behind Netflix (~300M+) and roughly in the Disney+/Peacock tier; but a top-tier content owner by IP depth (HBO prestige TV, DC, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, Looney Tunes) and one of the largest Hollywood film/TV studios by output and box office share.

moat_factors.description: HBO/HBO Max consistently wins the most prestige-TV awards (9 Emmy wins for The Penguin, 5 for The Pitt in 2025) and commands premium positioning versus ad-driven competitors

One of the largest film/TV libraries in the world (DC, Wizarding World, Game of Thrones, Looney Tunes, Hanna-Barbera) enabling content licensing, theme parks, games and franchise extension independent of any single platform
Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group/Television Group is a top-tier Hollywood studio with consistent theatrical hit rate, but competes for the same finite pool of creative talent as every other studio
Cable/satellite carriage agreements still generate the single largest profit pool (Global Linear Networks), but cord-cutting erodes this moat every year (domestic linear subscribers -9% in 2025)

weaknesses: Heavy financial leverage from the 2022 WarnerMedia/Discovery merger constrained content spending flexibility versus better-capitalized rivals (Netflix, Disney, Amazon)
Streaming subscriber base and global footprint smaller than Netflix/Disney, limiting negotiating leverage with advertisers and content partners
Lost NBA broadcast rights (effective 2025/2026), removing a key live-sports draw for Global Linear Networks/TNT Sports in the U.S.
Linear advertising and affiliate revenue in structural decline with no durable offset yet from streaming at the segment-profit level

Repeated, costly strategic indecision in 2025-2026 (planned Warner Bros./Discovery Global separation, a Netflix deal that was signed, amended, and then terminated at a $2.8B cash cost) signaled weak board/management conviction before the PSKY deal

growth_drivers: International HBO Max rollout - passed 100 markets in 2025, launched Germany/Italy Jan 2026, UK targeted March 2026
Streaming profitability inflection - Streaming segment Adjusted EBITDA grew from $677M (2024) to $1,370M (2025) on subscriber growth and cost discipline
Theatrical/franchise strength - DC Studios reboot (Superman) and non-DC hits (A Minecraft Movie, Sinners, Weapons) drove a 9% increase in Studios content revenue in 2025
Cost restructuring across Global Linear Networks and Corporate to protect EBITDA amid linear decline

Strategic exit via M&A - after an aborted self-directed separation (Warner Bros./Discovery Global) and a failed Netflix deal, the business ultimately realized shareholder value through an outright sale to Paramount Skydance at a premium to the pre-process share price

For the acquirer (Paramount Skydance/Skydance Corp.): combining WBD's HBO/Max platform, film/TV library and studio infrastructure with Paramount's own studio, CBS and cable assets to build a ~$70B-revenue, 200M+ streaming-subscriber global media company able to compete at scale with Netflix and Disney

business.description: Domestic linear subscribers -9% and ad audience -25% in 2025; Global Linear Networks Adjusted EBITDA fell 21% YoY, and declines were expected to continue
Absence of the NBA depressed 2026 advertising revenue and audience at Global Linear Networks/TNT Sports

business.risk: Content/talent competition and hit-driven Studios results
business.description: Studios Adjusted EBITDA swung sharply quarter to quarter based on film slate timing and comparisons to prior-year hits

financial.risk: High leverage from the WarnerMedia/Discovery merger
financial.description: Total debt of $32.8B at YE2025 (down from higher post-merger peaks after $23.5B of 2025 repurchases/repayments); S&P, Moody's and Fitch downgraded WBD ratings in 2025 citing linear weakness and leverage
A $15-17B Bridge Loan Facility (from 2025 tender offers) required refinancing before its (extended) June 2027 maturity; execution risk if capital markets conditions worsened
$2.8B cash paid to Netflix in 2026 to exit the Netflix Merger Agreement in favor of the PSKY deal, a direct cash drag recorded in Q1 2026

regulatory.risk: Antitrust challenge to the PSKY Merger
regulatory.description: In July 2026, 12 state attorneys general and the WGA sued in the N.D. Cal. to block the merger under Clayton Act Section 7; a September 2026 settlement (behavioral remedies, a News Editorial Independence Board for CNN/CBS, minimum film-output commitments for 5 years) cleared the way to close, though the WGA separately said it would continue its own suit
Deal required clearance in nearly 70 jurisdictions worldwide before closing

macro.description: Linear and streaming ad revenue sensitive to macro ad spend and sports/content slate timing
International streaming and network operations create EUR/GBP and other currency exposure

execution.description: Board pursued, in sequence, a Warner Bros./Discovery Global separation, a Netflix acquisition of Streaming & Studios, and finally the PSKY sale of the whole company within about 12 months (mid-2025 to early 2026) - costly and distracting

execution.severity: moderate (now the acquirer's risk, not WBD's)
execution.description: Combining WBD's content/platform organization with Paramount's under new leadership (David Ellison as CEO, Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO) carries standard large-scale M&A integration risk, now borne by Skydance Corporation (SKYD) shareholders rather than WBD's former shareholders, who were cashed out

macro_factors.industry_outlook: U.S. linear pay-TV continues to shrink annually (high single-digit to low double-digit subscriber declines industry-wide) while global streaming remains a growth category that is maturing and consolidating; the WBD/Paramount deal and the preceding failed WBD/Netflix deal were themselves evidence of accelerating industry consolidation as scale became viewed as a competitive necessity against Netflix and Disney.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - advertising and theatrical box office are cyclical/discretionary; subscription streaming and affiliate fees are more recurring, though increasingly price-sensitive.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High (historically) given WBD's large floating/fixed debt load and reliance on capital markets access and credit ratings; this sensitivity transferred to Skydance Corporation's balance sheet upon acquisition.
key_input_costs: Talent/creative labor (subject to WGA/SAG-AFTRA collective bargaining)

recent_developments.event: Domestic wholesale streaming distribution deal renewed on less favorable terms, pressuring Global ARPU
WBD announced plans to separate into two public companies: Warner Bros. (Streaming & Studios) and Discovery Global (Global Linear Networks)
Board broadened strategic review to include a sale of the whole company or separate transactions for each half, alongside continuing the separation
PSKY (Paramount Skydance Corporation) launched a tender offer for WBD; WBD filed a Schedule 14D-9 recommendation statement
WBD entered an amended Netflix Merger Agreement under which Netflix would acquire the Streaming & Studios business (HBO Max, HBO, film/TV studios) following a separation/spin-off of Discovery Global
PSKY sued WBD's board in Delaware Chancery Court alleging fiduciary-duty disclosure failures tied to its tender offer; case dismissed with prejudice by 2026-03-02 per the eventual merger agreement

WBD's board found PSKY's offer a 'Company Superior Proposal,' terminated the Netflix Merger Agreement (triggering a $2.8B cash termination fee paid by PSKY on WBD's behalf) and signed the PSKY Merger Agreement at $31.00/share cash plus a ticking fee after 2026-09-30; Larry Ellison personally guaranteed $45.72B of the consideration
WBD stockholders approved the PSKY Merger Agreement

Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America (West and East) sued in the N.D. Cal. to block the merger on antitrust (Clayton Act Section 7) grounds; parties agreed to a standstill on closing pending resolution

Paramount Skydance settled with the state attorneys general: five years of behavioral remedies, a News Editorial Independence Board covering CNN and CBS News, and minimum annual film-release commitments (30 films/year rising to 32, including at least 4 independent films), clearing the main obstacle to closing; the WGA indicated it would continue its own separate suit

Deal closed: WBD shareholders received $31.01666668/share in cash; WBD stock and senior notes delisted from Nasdaq; combined company renamed Skydance Corporation, began trading on NYSE as SKYD under CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz

guidance.as_of: N/A - WBD was acquired and delisted on 2026-10-06; it no longer issues guidance
guidance.management_commentary: Formal forward guidance was effectively suspended through most of 2025-2026 while the board ran a sequential strategic process (self-directed separation -> Netflix sale of Streaming & Studios -> PSKY sale of the whole company). The last standalone operating commentary (Q2 2026 10-Q) emphasized continued HBO Max international expansion (UK launch targeted March 2026), Streaming segment profitability improvement, and continued expected declines in linear subscribers/advertising, all now superseded by the closed acquisition. Any current guidance for the combined business would come from Skydance Corporation (SKYD), not from WBD.

bull_case: Reframed as 'why Paramount Skydance paid up for WBD': HBO/Max is widely regarded as the most prestige, awards-winning streaming content brand, giving the combined company a premium anchor versus Netflix/Disney

WBD brought one of the deepest owned IP libraries in media (DC, Wizarding World, Game of Thrones, Looney Tunes, Hanna-Barbera) plus a top-tier film/TV production studio, filling gaps in Paramount's own content portfolio

Combining WBD's ~131.6M streaming subscribers and global HBO Max rollout with Paramount+ created a company management described as having 200M+ streaming subscribers and ~$70B of combined revenue, positioned to compete at Netflix/Disney scale

The $31.01666668/share all-cash deal, personally guaranteed in large part by Larry Ellison, delivered WBD shareholders a known, certain cash outcome rather than continued execution risk on a leveraged standalone turnaround
The multi-bidder process (Netflix vs. PSKY) demonstrated real strategic value in WBD's assets, with PSKY ultimately outbidding and winning after a competitive Superior Proposal process
bear_case: Reframed as standalone WBD's weaknesses as of its last reporting period: linear networks (still ~73% of segment Adjusted EBITDA) were in uninterrupted structural decline with no proven offsetting streaming-profit scale

High leverage from the 2022 WarnerMedia/Discovery merger (still $32.8B of debt at YE2025 despite aggressive 2025 deleveraging) constrained content investment and drew multiple 2025 credit-rating downgrades
Loss of NBA rights and ongoing domestic ad audience erosion (-25% in 2025) showed the linear advertising base deteriorating faster than streaming could compensate

Governance/strategy whiplash - a public separation plan, a signed-then-terminated Netflix deal costing $2.8B in cash, and board litigation from a disappointed bidder (PSKY) - reflected weak strategic conviction in the year before the sale

Regulatory risk was real and nearly derailed the deal: a 12-state-AG and WGA antitrust suit forced a closing standstill and only cleared via a September 2026 settlement imposing five years of behavioral remedies (editorial independence boards, film-output quotas) on the surviving company, risk now borne by SKYD rather than WBD shareholders, who had already been cashed out
